wy_sinks_canyon.blurb: Sinks Canyon cuts into the southern Wind River Mountains just outside Lander. Sport climbing is the main draw, mostly 5.10 to 5.12 with a few easier lines and a handful of harder ones, and the steep dolomite walls carry most of it, with pocketed and overhanging faces at places like Killer Cave and Hardware Wall. Trad is found on the granite and sandstone, and bouldering spreads across all three rock types, from V0 up to double digits. The cliffs face south, so they catch the sun and stay climbable through much of the year; cooler months are the most comfortable. Fairfield Hill and Shady Side hold the biggest concentrations of routes, and most walls are a short walk from the road.

pa_southwestern_highlands.blurb: Southwestern Pennsylvania's climbing is spread across the Laurel Highlands, the Youghiogheny River country around Ohiopyle, and the hills near Pittsburgh. Bouldering dominates, with problems from V0 to V5 making up the bulk and a thin tail of much harder ones, set on sandstone in wooded boulderfields. Roped climbing is the smaller share: short sport, trad and top-rope lines, mostly 5.7 to 5.11, with a few ice and mixed routes in winter. Ohiopyle State Park is the biggest single area, with The Lost Crag, Breakneck and Beam Rocks among the other notable names. Crags are scattered over a wide, mostly rural region, so expect a lot of driving between them.

nh_lakes_region.blurb: The Lakes Region sits around the big lakes of central New Hampshire, with climbing scattered through small hill crags and boulder zones rather than one big cliff. Bouldering is the largest share, mostly V0 to V5 with a few hard problems, and Bayle Mountain and Oak Mountain are the main boulder areas. Trad comes next, usually 5.5 to 5.11, with the New Durham area holding the most routes. Sport climbing is limited but present, notably at Sandwich Notch, a quiet brookside cliff band where the routes tend to be on the harder side and top-rope sites and boulders sit nearby. A modest number of winter ice routes round out the picture.

wa_northeast_corner_spokane.blurb: This is the climbing of Washington's far northeast, centred on the city of Spokane, where most of the climbs are packed into the Spokane Area and a few smaller outposts sit farther north at Metaline Falls, Marcus, China Bend and Onion Creek. Sport routes dominate, running mostly from 5.8 to 5.12 and centred on 5.10 and 5.11. Trad and bouldering each make up a smaller share, and there are some top-rope lines and a few mixed routes. Minnehaha is the established trad and bouldering spot near town, and Deep Creek is a steep sport crag on basalt. Many areas are close enough to the city for a short outing after work.

ca_pinto_basin.blurb: Pinto Basin covers the eastern and southern side of Joshua Tree National Park, and it feels quieter than the busier parts of the park, with some remote formations. Traditional climbing is by far the main activity, with a decent amount of sport, some top-rope routes and a small amount of bouldering. Grades run from easy 5.0 climbs to the occasional 5.13, but the weight sits around 5.8 to 5.11, so it suits climbers working through the moderate and middle grades. Split Rocks is the largest cluster, followed by Jumbo Rock Area, Stirrup Tank and the OZ Area. Desert heat makes summer difficult.

co_independence_pass.blurb: Independence Pass climbing lines the high road east of Aspen, with crags between roughly 9,000 and 11,000 feet and a side valley at Lincoln Creek. The rock is a mix of compact granite and gneiss that often makes for steep, overhanging lines. Sport and trad split fairly evenly, mostly 5.8 to 5.12, and there is a large bouldering scene running from V0 up to V10 and beyond. Grotto Walls, the Upper Boulderfield, Lincoln Creek and Monitor Rock are the biggest areas. Most crags hold only a handful of routes and sit a short walk from the road, so you can sample a few in a day. Walls tend to face south and get hot, so this is mainly a summer area.
